title: HttpClient with a Service
summary: Move your API calls into a service that components can share.
heading: HttpClient with a Service

sections.title: Why put HttpClient in a service?

blocks.text: In Chapter 35 we called the API straight from a component. That's fine for one screen, but the URL and request logic get copied around as the app grows. Move them into a service: one place owns the API, and every component just asks it for data.
Inject HttpClient once, keep the base URL in one spot, and expose a method per operation. Each returns an Observable — the request runs when something subscribes.

blocks.label: user.service.ts

sections.title: Example 1 & 2: read all and read one

blocks.text: The component injects the service and subscribes. It holds no URL and no HTTP code.

blocks.label: list.ts

blocks.text: Create and update send an object; delete takes an id. After a change, refresh the list (or update the signal locally).

blocks.label: list.ts

blocks.text: Because the service returns an Observable, the component decides how to handle waiting and failure — usually with a couple of signals.

blocks.label: list.ts

blocks.text: Tip: the async pipe can subscribe for you — @if (users.getAll() | async; as list) { ... } — though caching the Observable in a field is better than calling it in the template.

items: Put HttpClient and the API URL in a service, not the component.
Expose one method per operation, each returning an Observable.
Components inject the service and subscribe — they stay thin.
The same service is reused by every component that needs the data.
Handle loading/errors in the component (or via the async pipe).
